extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Restoration drama, literary critics, and playwrights interested in play reception and craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for writing, adapting, and judging Restoration comedies (reasons for a play's success or failure, theatrical effects, audience reception, and satire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as mode of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: "originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that originality should be judged by how a playwright handles material rather than whether the subject itself is new (Langbaine's criticism confuses subject with treatment). Use novel approach and treatment to claim originality even when themes are familiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a 'lameness of the action' (weak plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author in the dedication hints at the "lameness of the action" as a cause of the play's unpopularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lively, well-constructed action/plot is required; a weak or listless plot ('lameness') can provoke audience dislike regardless of other merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not provoke unintended political or religious offence
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's second title, "Love in a Nunnery," caused suspicions that the author intended to ridicule the Duke of York and the Catholic religion, which may have contributed to its poor reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about titles, themes, or jokes that could be read as attacks on powerful persons or sensitive institutions; perceived topical offence can alienate audiences even if the text contains nothing to justify the suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absurd or vulgar stage business (inelegant 'jeu de theatre')
rubrics_metrics.description: "Perhaps the absurd and vulgar scene, in which the prince pretends a fit of the cholic, had some share in occasioning the fall of the piece. This inelegant jeu de theatre is severely ridiculed..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical devices and physical gags should be tasteful and well-judged; crude or inelegant stage antics can ruin audience esteem and be singled out by critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for performance and production quality (actors share responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poet and performers are nearly equally involved in the disgrace of a condemned piece" — performers and the poet are both implicated in a play's failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play's success depends as much on actors, direction and production as on the writing; authors and companies should recognise shared responsibility and the potential for misattribution of blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize audience caprice and factional tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectators' capricious condemnation may have no good reason; different audiences (court vs city) respond differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect unpredictability in reception; consider the distinct preferences of audience segments (e.g., court vs city), and that public taste can be fickle or politically/ socially influenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer example-driven, lively moralizing over dull didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Epilogue: "Not with dull morals, gravely writ, like those, Which men of easy phlegm with care compose... But by examples drawn... From most of you who hear and see the play."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a play aims to reform or moralize, do so through vivid examples and satire rooted in the audience's experience rather than stiff, preachy moralizing; entertain while instructing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance severity of satire and maintain authorial self-awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: "He would not quite the women's frailty bare, But stript them to the waist, and left them there: And the men's faults are less severely shown, For he considers that himself is one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate the harshness of satire; an author who exposes others' vices but acknowledges his own faults avoids appearing vindictive or hypocritical. Restraint and self-awareness can preserve audience goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations/translations must be handled with care (avoid 'mangling')
rubrics_metrics.description: Ravenscroft "translated and mangled several of the more farcical French comedies" and his versions were mocked; poor appropriation invites ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or translating foreign plays, preserve craft and spirit; careless or heavy-handed alteration of source material can result in critical contempt and audience rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misplaced or dated comic devices that distract from the play
rubrics_metrics.description: The text singles out an 'inelegant jeu de theatre' (the prince's simulated cholic) as an example of a comic device that drew ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic set-pieces should feel appropriate to the play's tone and audience expectations; contrived or awkward jokes/stunts can undermine credibility and provoke derision rather than laughter.
